Nurses in particular are prized - nurses are leaving the profession faster than schools can produce NP/BSN/RN/LPNs. I was pleased to see so many books on the list that I had enjoyed while growing up in the late 1960s through 1970s, especially “Wind in the Willows” and “Stuart Little.” But it also doesn’t entirely surprise me that Munro Leaf’s “The Story of Ferdinand” — my favorite childhood book — didn’t make the cut.

As the only Jewish kid in my Oregon high school, I was unfamiliar with the New Testament. When excerpts were part of the assigned reading in my senior literature class I found some of the differences between Christian and Jewish teachings to be confounding. Meanwhile, my Christian classmates nodded in comfortable understanding. (Of course, as the only Jewish kid in the school, I couldn’t really ask questions about this in class, both because of the sense of feeling like the odd one out and because no one there would have been of much help.)

The goals of this list are clear: make children into devoted readers, while also inculcating them to a set of values that are on the whole positive, but can leave some kids feeling like they’re a few steps outside of the social weal. That has always been a challenge in a country as large and as diverse as ours. 

I can only hope that, along with this reading list, the students are given the chance to discuss, argue with and learn from each other as they develop the critical thinking skills that will serve them well in adulthood.

comments.body: I live in Texas and have two elementary school-age children in public school. I find this list acceptable, especially the inclusion of biblical passages. Even though I am an atheist, I agree that familiarity with the Bible is required for thoroughly appreciating a large swath of literature (e.g., who can appreciate Dostoevsky’s The Idiot without having read the Bible?). That said, our household will clearly add other religious texts, authors from different backgrounds, and more contemporary literature to this list. As a jumping off point for a Texan, though, it is fine. The exclusion of To Kill A Mockingbird is disheartening, and I would be curious to see the record on why they chose to exclude it. Excluding Toni Morrison, too, is disheartening, but as long as Texas doesn’t tell me that I can’t have my children read whatever they want outside of the classroom, what really is the problem? And “banning” books really just highlights them as intriguing for the kids, so ban away, because we have the Internet and agency.

comments.name: Lou
comments.body:
As many have pointed out, the list includes many wonderful classics, but skews right. 

However, as a retired English teacher, I’m more concerned about the appropriate age level for some of these titles.  Do you really think 6th graders will be able to fully grasp Ulysses S. Grant’s “General Order 108 to the ‘Soldiers of the Armies of the United States’” or “The Gettysburg Address”?   I love “The Outsiders”, but it’s more appropriate for high school than 7th grade.   I’d argue the same for “ Do Not Go Gentle Into That Good Night” and “ The Road Not Taken.”   And, Dante’s “Inferno” in 10th grade?  Seriously? The list goes on.  These are wonderful texts, but a couple of years makes a huge difference for young people.  

You might counter that some of these poems or texts are short, so what’s the big deal?  I’ll counter by saying that there’s no room for wasting time, effort, or lessons.  A steady drip of inaccessible texts is a real turn off to student achievement.  Take it from someone who taught (or tried to) excerpts from Gandhi’s “Salt March Speech” to 10th graders. It’s hard to instill a love of reading, which should be a goal in education, with the scheduling of some of these texts.

Instead of just two…

I remember there was a quiz placing folks in 4 political tribes via the 4 quadrants of 2 independent dimensions “social” versus “economic” views.

To go to 8 from 4 would have just been 3 “independent” dimensions, and the endpoints of the corresponding cube (though we’d have 3 different things breaking up apart the prior 2 instead of including them as axes).

In reality, when you survey how people feel about n different (not necessarily independent) topics, you are bound to get at least 2^n responses upon surveying sufficiently many people.  That doesn’t mean that there are exponentially many “tribes” but that tribalism is not that expressive.

And, so, unable to optimize the precise tribalist configuation, we just return to the original two.

It is necessarily chaotic and illogical, but the important thing becomes: Does the right* decision happen at the right moment?

That is all that is important.  Even words change quickly with time, so let’s not be too attached to them.

[*] Ironically, very often not “right wing” though.

Communication, explanations and sharing are the only way to get a message understood and the collaboration of the people. A little modesty & respect from "experts & deciders" can go a long way. 

Allow me an example. 

In Switzerland where I live politicians went on TV to discuss the COVID issue, admitting that because novel, the approach needed to be flexible as we learned more. Health officials discussed contrasting needs with local politicians, schools, businesses and others to understand and find best comprise solutions. Rules set but evolved as needed. 
- Businesses (except groceries) were closed early, gradually reopened. 
- Schools were closed the first months but elementary to middle schools reopened with adaptations because younger children absolutely need the interactions (& are not as vulnerable). 
- When limited vaccines became available, doctors were asked to evaluate their patients' risks & enrol the most needy for the first vaccines. 

Every week leaders adapted as needed and communicated their reasoning/rationale for adding or lifting restrictions. It wasn't easy but most were happy to do what was needed. High-school & university students immediately organised to bring groceries to the elderly and needy, military were sent to support logistics in care homes & hospitals, for instance.

I can still remember one particular moment when I was on an underground train in Hong Kong when Covid first came out there. All the passengers wore a mask - some wore two. That was quite a sight never seen before. You could see fear in their eyes - all of them. And in a hugely over-populated city like Hong Kong all of these people wanted to keep a respectable distance from their fellow passengers as if they were all untouchables. What a sight - all of a sudden human nature (certainly not the best bit) played out. And I think this 'rage' thing can best be explained when we remind ourselves what 'human nature' really means.

She loved it, but thought it was too fancy for her lifestyle. They moved on to the next city on their vacation itinerary. But she couldn't get that ring out of her head. So my dad called the jeweler and somehow the ring was obtained and she returned home with it.  I had never seen the ring before as it sat in the safety deposit box at the bank.  I asked for what occasions did she pull the ring from the bank?  She answered none. She never wore it because to her it was just too fancy, even for the weddings and other formal occasions she and dad would frequent. Mom lived frugally and the many pieces of jewelry she gave me rarely saw the light of day. I am grateful for them, and I am beginning to incorporate them into my regular rotation. I agree Israel must be held accountable for the staggering death and destruction in Gaza. That reckoning is necessary and overdue. 

But framing this war as a “win” for Israel, without reckoning with how it began, is a moral sleight of hand. This war started with Hamas’s own genocidal intensions, as it invaded Israeli communities to kidnap, murder, and rape civilians in their homes.

Israeli society has not walked away unscathed. For months, families didn’t know if loved ones were alive in tunnels beneath Gaza. Sirens and rockets became the soundtrack of daily life throughout Israel. And for years, Hamas denied the Red Cross access to hostages while releasing footage of starved, broken captives, not as a byproduct of war, but a deliberate act of psychological cruelty.

So yes, Israel suffered fewer casualties and less territorial ruin than Gaza. But is that really victory? A traumatized society, a hostage crisis that hollowed out the nation’s psyche, and an international reputation now deeply damaged. These aren’t the marks of a winner. They’re wounds that will outlast this war for years.

None of this erases Israel’s own responsibility for the scale of suffering in Gaza. But accountability has to run in both directions. Hamas still refuses to disarm or relinquish power, prolonging Gazans’ suffering along with Israel’s. Real moral clarity means holding everyone who caused and prolonged this catastrophe to account, not just the side easier to condemn from a distance.

comments.body:
I’m an app developer — I make Punge (on-device NSFW detection) and BingeWatch (movie/show tracking). Built both before AI; since then I’ve used it mainly to add features and speed up debugging, not to build from scratch.

The download numbers here say it all: apps up 100%, downloads up 2%. AI didn’t fix the App Store’s real problem — it just added more competitors to an already broken discovery system. The top 1% of publishers have long captured roughly 80% of downloads and 90%+ of revenue. That was true before vibecoding, and it’s still true now.

Ranking for anything competitive is pay-to-play. Venture-backed teams outbid indies on keywords before an indie app even shows up in search. A few hundred or a few thousand dollars in ads doesn’t scratch the surface. So sure, it’s never been easier to build an app — but it’s not any easier to get someone to find it. If anything it’s harder, because now you’re buried under hundreds of thousands more apps just like yours. The App Store didn’t get more democratic. It got more crowded.

When I grew up in Germany and France in the seventies and eighties, I learnt, even in elementary school, about diarrhea-inducing pathogens, that were spread because at the time (this is no longer the case naturally) small farmers were using the contents of their own outhouses as fertilizer for their produce.
This wasn't considered an exception, but the rule, and the quality of the produce wasn't disdained, but cherished, since these were small-scale farmers who didn't use pesticides or artificial fertilizer and hand-picked everything themselves.
Everything that grew on the ground, not on trees, and especially leafy vegetables, herbs, and some berries, were vulnerable, so we understood, as nine-year-old kids, to rigorously wash produce in water, changed a couple of times, and whenever there were regional outbreaks, we were told to blanch, boil, sear everything.
A raspberry galette or pie, putting the herbs on top of a boiling soup or stew, lettuce soup, radicchio risotto, grilled caesar salad (yes, the romaine too), stir-fried cucumbers (these are all American serious eats or nyt cooking recipes by the way) - you can eat everything heated just enough to kill cyclospora but still summer-appropriate, healthy, and totally delicious.
Yes, it's a bit more work than mixing pre-washed salad mixes with ready-made salad dressings, but it's so worth it, for taste as well as health...

The survey of Odyssey translations, especially by non-readers of ancient Greek, always perplexes me in its insufficiency. To say that a translation gives the English "feel" of Homeric poetry is to be linguistically and prosodically oxymoronic. One must never forget Robert Frost’s definition of poetry as “that which is lost in translation” by which he means “inevitably lost” (therefore scratch, e.g., Fitzgerald, the darling of secondary school teachers who know no Greek). Chapman’s antique translation (enshrined by Keats) is robust and, more occasionally than most, accurate enough). Rieu, Fagles, and Wilson (and Fitzgerald and Chapman too) give what Nabokov would call paraphrases rather than translations.
Missing from so many marches through Odyssey translations are what are arguably the two best: T.E. Shaw (= T.E. Lawrence of Arabia) and Richmond Lattimore, both of whom have an impeccable knowledge of Greek. In addition, Lattimore (a long-time profeesor of Greek at Bryn Mawr College) was a good poet. Shaw/Lawrence gives a prose translation that is very faithful to the Greek (even if it is a bit Britishy), while Lattimore manages to provide a translation that is both accurate and in a majestic verse form that minimizes the need for linguistic compromises to the prosody. Give students Shaw/Lawrence first, and encourage them later to re-read in Lattimore.

We find non-stops a must, and order a special meal  (ie fruit plate) if any meal at all, to avoid smelly food trays, and bring good snacks. Not only do you not adequately describe the critical role of the lymphatic system (clearing the body of toxins), your descriptions of how to do massage are ridiculous.  You don’t massage up your face. You could have done a real service to folks by describing lymphedema in terms of its causes such as cancer surgery and other surgeries and how it affects folks.  Instead you make it seem like an inconvenient problem of puffy face.  For other articles you provide really long introductory materials describing the problem in detail, but for this one, you gloss over all the introductory stuff.  You have done a real disservice to the almost 33% of folks who develop lymphedema because of cancer surgery or other surgeries.  And you make it seem like an inconvenience rather than the debilitating condition that it really is.  You could have really educated people here.  A total missed opportunity. comments.name: cz
comments.body:
I've battled lymphedema for 18 years after cancer surgery and treatment.  Now in my "golden years" it has gotten worse.  

Exercise too little -- swollen ankles.  Exercise too much -- swollen ankles.  Diet doesn't seem to matter.  Compression socks and braces -- hurt and are ineffective. 

 I finally qualified for a lymphedema pump.  It works, but takes an hour in the morning and an hour at night, consistently, to have any long-term effects for more than a day.  And qualifying for a pump has taken years, after spending a lot of my own money on lymphedema specialists, socks, etc.  

Now I have veins that need fixing from the strain on my calfs.  And I have to take water pills to drain the fluid (that make you pee all the time).  

I doubt this method on the face and neck will do any good.  Just like the creams and eye pads you put under your eyes to reduce puffiness.  A temporary fix for a night out.

I took the 'water' pills for several days, with increased urine output. The swelling decreased. I have not yet gone back to the pills and my feet have not regained their swelling. Based on what I said at the beginning, it is likely that the source is Lymph fluid, as the damage to my Lymph system could lead to that. If true, that means that for those with extra swelling from Lymphatic fluid should consider so called 'water' pills.

This protest has long ceased to be about students. It has become a stage for disruption, with every attempt seemingly aimed at provoking chaos in the hope that any ugly incident can be weaponized against the Indian government.

Foreign funding and outside interests have an uncanny way of finding willing activists eager to keep the pot boiling, regardless of the cost to students or the country. The leakage of exam questions is a serious issue. Is it a new problem? No, this has occurred several times before. The issue is systemic; it's similar to counterfeit currency—someone finds a way to defeat the system. In a very large country, the likelihood of such problems arising is quite high.

Will Wangchuk's hunger strike solve the problem? I don’t believe it will. Will stone-pelting resolve the issue? Unlikely. Could a totalitarian government address the problem? Perhaps, but it would be a risky experiment, and once initiated, it may take a long time to reverse. Russia's attempts have failed, while China's might be considered successful. Should India follow the Chinese model? Most would likely say no.

Mindless protests, like those that seem to occur frequently in India, act as pressure-release valves. They highlight flaws within the system, but they also overshadow the successes. Is India a better country now than it was 12 years ago? Definitely. The country is clearly making progress, although not as quickly as we might hope. The comparison is between India, with its constant agitations, and China, which has none.

The agitators are asking for the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, the Education Minister, or Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Who will they replace them with?

comments.body: When we bought our PA home 4 years ago, part of the purchase deal was that we needed to assume the remaining 20 years on the solar panels lease. We were considering purchasing a battery backup system, and the end of the tax incentives had us move the installation forward into 2025.  The major downside with (our) solar is the system is designed to stop generating power during an outage, to protect the utility workers from power generated by solar.  Our batteries now allow us to harness the juice from our panels during an outage.  We do pay a monthly connectivity fee to the utility to subsidize them for our use of the grid, and during most mid-spring to mid-fall months, that connectivity fee is the only cost on our utility bill. We seem to be at a pivotal point in the history of warfare yet again (sadly, we could say, but here we are).  It seems this struggle is linked to the implications:

Unmanned, relatively cheap, drones on land, in water and in the air have greatly changed the nature of this war.  It has allowed Ukraine to neutralize massed attacks by Russia on land and at sea (i.e. traditional naval control of the Black Sea + massed troops and tanks on land).  In the air, Russia still sadly has the ballistic missiles to attack Ukrainian cities unanswered ... so far.   At the same time, Ukraine has achieved significant aerial success itself.

But where does this leave the "2023-4" questions of this war that the generals may cling to?  Have military innovations rendered those issues redundant or less important?
1. Russia conventional ammunition advantage (e.g. shells)
2. access to modern fighter jets
3. troop numbers, training, attrition and morale
4. Trump as an explicit or tacit Russian ally
5. the roles of NATO, Iran, China and North Korea
6. Internet access - e.g. Starlink

The only questions that appear to be settled are:
1. tanks will play no further role in this war
2. yes Ukraine can, and will, strike deep within Russia
3. defense systems such as patriot missiles are still needed
4. Crimea will not be recaptured (liberated) but Ukraine can greatly disrupt Russian governance there.
5. the United States is not a reliable ally ... for Ukraine, for Russia or for anyone else.

If we had to wade into "Continental" Philosophy (how quaint), that meant Leibniz - but only because he had "something" to do with Locke and Hume - and, of course, Kant, because, well, Kant.

Wittgenstein, to  a great extent, was somehow transnational and at Cambridge, so may as well have been Anglo, too.

But fifty years later, these ghosts of my youth still linger, and their aging tomes still surround me in this room. What I can no longer find, sadly, is someone with whom I can talk about them.

And when I try to tell anyone younger, in this day and age, "Major in philosophy; whatever happens in your life, you'll be a happier older person some day..." Well, you can imagine how that goes down...

Oh well... Vive la différence!

Bayreuth is a, or at last can be, a life-changing experience for classical music fans.
While this article is great, I want to disperse some more practical advice I've given to international Bayreuth Festival visitors:
Dress in linen (and/or cool/summer wool or silk) in black, for women with flat, open shoes (cobblestone ground, uneven stairs) - for guys, wear kind of what James Bond does when in a tropical location in the casino, something like Brioni's Leggera tuxedo from linen and silk, with a linen shirt, or something similar. 
For women, I can tell you what I've worn - long black silk wide pants and a completely backless linen tank top, with (high-end) flip-flops, and wear your hair up or in a ponytail. And bring something to cover up in the evening or for the halls, which will be considerably cooler.
Bring a spare top, which you change into in the long break - I mean it, you'll be drenched, and really thankful to change into something fresh and clean.
Bring a nice fan (to use and as part of your look), even the guys, and a chair cushion that doesn't make sounds (test at home) when you change positions.
Get a rental car and look for a nice (even spa) hotel not in Bayreuth, but in the surrounding areas, even up to beautiful Nuremberg (one hour by car).
If you're serious about it, get slowly comfortable with very high temperatures without a/c - don't underestimate 5 hours in summer heat, without a/c, with closed doors, no draft, on hard wooden chairs.
And be on time.

This is a particularly bad time to be dismantling both our ability to respond to intensifying climate change-related impacts and our ability to forecast extreme weather events.

During a recent summer the tropical storm Otis was near Acapulco in the morning and that evening it made landfall in the city as a catastrophic category 5 hurricane.

It used to be that hurricanes would churn up cooler water at depth which reduced the rate of intensification (hurricanes derive their strength from warm water). Now as the deeper water warms this effect is reduced; so the hotter that we make the ocean the more rapid the ensuing intensification and the higher the maximum storm strength.

Imagine a tropical storm not far from Miami being largely ignored then mere hours later landing as a category 5 hurricane.

With maximum storm strength increasing we need more than ever the best ability we can muster to respond to disasters and to forecast these events that we can manage.
